conventional.policy_description: Extend the IRA clean energy credits five years beyond the 2032 sunset. No official score: published figures cover the credits as enacted or their repeal, never a five-year extension. The figure shown is this calculator's own estimate.

credibility.no_band_reason: no pre-registered row scores a carbon price or an energy credit
limitations: holdout labels follow the locked post-2026-05-02 regression protocol; they are not retroactive historical out-of-sample claims.
No pre-registered out-of-sample row scores a policy of this class, so this model's accuracy on one has not been measured.
CBO's 2024 figure is a projection of uncapped-credit uptake that has already moved by roughly a factor of two since 2022; treating it as a fixed benchmark understates its own uncertainty.

Not a published benchmark: climate.py documents carbon_tax_behavioral_factor as calibrated so that $50/ton yields ~$1.7T, and the target restates that. Scoring against it measures internal consistency only.
No interaction with income or payroll receipts (a carbon tax erodes its own base and the income-tax base simultaneously) and no rebate or revenue-recycling design is modelled.

Scored as a $7,500 credit on a 1.5M-vehicle base growing 15%/yr; the income and vehicle-price caps, the separate used (25E) and commercial (45W) credits, and the demand response to withdrawing the subsidy are not modelled.

Adding the used-vehicle credit (sec. 25E, $7.4B) would give $189.8B. For scale on how far this number has travelled, the repo's own knowledge base still gives a $30-60B range on the 2022 baseline and JCX-18-22 scored the same credits at $14.2B over FY2022-2031.
credibility.caption: No out-of-sample band: no pre-registered row scores a carbon price or an energy credit. The 44 pre-registered Tier 1 rows are the only tier that measures this model's accuracy, and none of them scores a policy of this kind.
